solution: Pascal's rule states \(\binom{n+1}{r}=\binom{n}{r-1}+\binom{n}{r}\). This is the standard recurrence for binomial coefficients. Hence (A).
The sum of all coefficients is found by substituting \(x=1\). Then \(\left(\dfrac{1}{1}+2(1)\right)^{6}=(1+2)^{6}=3^{6}=729\). Hence (B).

Using the binomial theorem, \(4^{n}-3n-1=(1+3)^{n}-3n-1=\sum_{k=2}^{n}\binom{n}{k}3^{k}=9\sum_{k=2}^{n}\binom{n}{k}3^{k-2}\), so every element of \(A\) is a multiple of 9. Listing: \(n=1\Rightarrow 0\), \(n=2\Rightarrow 9\), \(n=3\Rightarrow 54\). The set \(B=\{9(n-1):n\in N\}=\{0,9,18,27,\ldots\}\) is the set of all non-negative multiples of 9. Hence every element of \(A\) lies in \(B\), i.e. \(A\subset B\). Hence (C).

Expand and subtract: \((\sqrt{3}+1)^{2n}-(\sqrt{3}-1)^{2n}=2\sum_{k\ \text{odd}}\binom{2n}{k}(\sqrt{3})^{k}\). For odd \(k\), \((\sqrt{3})^{k}=3^{(k-1)/2}\sqrt{3}\), so each surviving term contains a factor \(\sqrt{3}\). The sum therefore is a non-zero multiple of \(\sqrt{3}\), which is irrational. Hence (C).

From \((1+1)^{n}=2^{n}=\sum\binom{n}{r}\) and \((1-1)^{n}=0=\sum(-1)^{r}\binom{n}{r}\), adding gives \(2(\binom{n}{0}+\binom{n}{2}+\binom{n}{4}+\cdots)=2^{n}\). Hence \(\binom{n}{0}+\binom{n}{2}+\cdots+\binom{n}{n}=2^{n-1}\). Hence (C).

Expanding, \((1+ax)^{n}=1+nax+\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}a^{2}x^{2}+\cdots\). Comparing coefficients: \(na=6\) and \(\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}a^{2}=\dfrac{27}{2}\Rightarrow n(n-1)a^{2}=27\). From \(na=6\), \(a=6/n\); substituting, \(n(n-1)\dfrac{36}{n^{2}}=27\Rightarrow \dfrac{36(n-1)}{n}=27\Rightarrow 36n-36=27n\Rightarrow 9n=36\Rightarrow n=4\), and \(a=6/4=\dfrac{3}{2}\). Hence (C).

The product of \(r\) consecutive integers \(n(n+1)\cdots(n+r-1)=\dfrac{(n+r-1)!}{(n-1)!}=\binom{n+r-1}{r}\cdot r!\), which is an integer multiple of \(r!\). Hence the product is always divisible by \(r!\). Hence (A).

Each bracket telescopes via Pascal's rule: \(\binom{7}{k}+\binom{7}{k+1}=\binom{8}{k+1}\). For \(k=0\) to \(6\), the sum is \(\binom{8}{1}+\binom{8}{2}+\cdots+\binom{8}{7}=2^{8}-\binom{8}{0}-\binom{8}{8}=2^{8}-2\). Hence (D).
Using the identity \(\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}^{2}=\binom{2n}{n}\), for \(n=5\) the value is \(\binom{10}{5}=252\). Hence (D).
In \((x+a)^{47}-(x-a)^{47}\), the terms with even powers of \(a\) cancel and only odd-power-of-\(a\) terms survive: powers \(a^{1},a^{3},\ldots,a^{47}\), i.e. \(\dfrac{47+1}{2}=24\) terms. Hence (A).

From \((1+x^{2})^{5}\) the available powers are \(x^{0}(1),x^{2}(5),x^{4}(10),\ldots\); from \((1+x)^{4}\) the powers are \(x^{0}\) to \(x^{4}\). To form \(x^{5}\): \(x^{4}\cdot x^{1}=10\cdot\binom{4}{1}=10\cdot 4=40\); \(x^{2}\cdot x^{3}=5\cdot\binom{4}{3}=5\cdot 4=20\). Total \(=40+20=60\). Hence (B).
The general term of \((1-2x)^{5}\) is \(\binom{5}{r}(-2x)^{r}\). For \(x^{4}\), \(r=4\): coefficient \(=\binom{5}{4}(-2)^{4}=5\cdot 16=80\). Hence (D).

Equating \(T_{7}=T_{8}\) in \((2a-3b)^{n}\): \(\binom{n}{6}(2a)^{n-6}(-3b)^{6}=\binom{n}{7}(2a)^{n-7}(-3b)^{7}\). Dividing, \(\binom{n}{6}(2a)=\binom{n}{7}(-3b)\Rightarrow \dfrac{2a}{-3b}=\dfrac{\binom{n}{7}}{\binom{n}{6}}=\dfrac{n-6}{7}\). Let \(t=\dfrac{2a}{3b}=\dfrac{6-n}{7}\). Then \(\dfrac{2a+3b}{2a-3b}=\dfrac{t+1}{t-1}=\dfrac{(13-n)/7}{(-1-n)/7}=\dfrac{13-n}{-(n+1)}=\dfrac{n-13}{n+1}\). Hence (A).

The general term of \(\left(x\cos\alpha+\dfrac{\sin\alpha}{x}\right)^{10}\) is \(\binom{10}{r}(x\cos\alpha)^{10-r}\left(\dfrac{\sin\alpha}{x}\right)^{r}\); independent of \(x\) when \(10-2r=0\Rightarrow r=5\). So the independent term \(=\binom{10}{5}\cos^{5}\alpha\sin^{5}\alpha=\binom{10}{5}(\sin\alpha\cos\alpha)^{5}=\binom{10}{5}\left(\dfrac{\sin 2\alpha}{2}\right)^{5}=\dfrac{\binom{10}{5}}{2^{5}}\sin^{5}2\alpha\). Its greatest value (at \(\sin 2\alpha=1\)) is \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{5}\binom{10}{5}\). Hence (B).

Factor \(1-x+x^{2}-x^{3}=(1+x^{2})(1-x)\), so the expression is \((1+x^{2})^{4}(1-x)^{4}\). Coefficient of \(x^{4}\): from \((1+x^{2})^{4}=\sum\binom{4}{j}x^{2j}\) (powers \(x^{0},x^{2},x^{4}\) with coefficients \(1,4,6\)) and \((1-x)^{4}=\sum\binom{4}{k}(-1)^{k}x^{k}\). Then coefficient of \(x^{4}=1\cdot\binom{4}{4}+4\cdot\binom{4}{2}+6\cdot\binom{4}{0}=1+24+6=31\). Hence (A).

Note \(1-\dfrac{2}{x}+\dfrac{4}{x^{2}}\) is a trinomial; the number of terms in its \(n\)-th power is \(\binom{n+2}{2}=\dfrac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}=28\Rightarrow (n+1)(n+2)=56\Rightarrow n=6\). The sum of all coefficients (put \(x=1\)) is \((1-2+4)^{6}=3^{6}=729\). Hence (D).
In \((x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-18)\), the coefficient of \(x^{17}\) (next-to-leading term) is the negative of the sum of the roots: \(-(1+2+\cdots+18)=-\dfrac{18\cdot 19}{2}=-171\). Hence (B).

In \((1+px)^n\), the coefficient of \(x\) is \(np=8\) and the coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(\binom{n}{2}p^2=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}p^2=24\). Dividing, \(\dfrac{(n-1)p}{2}=3\Rightarrow(n-1)p=6\). With \(np=8\): \(8-p=6\Rightarrow p=2\), \(n=4\). Hence (D).

There are 11 terms, so the middle term is the \(6^{\text{th}}\): \(T_{6}=\binom{10}{5}\left(\dfrac{10}{x}\right)^{5}\left(\dfrac{x}{10}\right)^{5}=\binom{10}{5}\cdot\dfrac{10^{5}}{x^{5}}\cdot\dfrac{x^{5}}{10^{5}}=\binom{10}{5}\). Hence (B).

The general term of \(\left(2+\dfrac{x}{3}\right)^{n}\) is \(\binom{n}{r}2^{n-r}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{r}x^{r}\). Equating coefficients of \(x^{5}\) and \(x^{6}\): \(\binom{n}{5}2^{n-5}3^{-5}=\binom{n}{6}2^{n-6}3^{-6}\Rightarrow \dfrac{\binom{n}{6}}{\binom{n}{5}}=\dfrac{2\cdot 3}{1}=6\Rightarrow \dfrac{n-5}{6}=6\Rightarrow n-5=36\Rightarrow n=41\). Hence (C).

The general term of \(\left(\sqrt{x}-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^{18}\) is \(\binom{18}{r}(\sqrt{x})^{18-r}\left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^{r}=\binom{18}{r}(-2)^{r}x^{(18-2r)/2}\). Independent of \(x\) when \(18-2r=0\Rightarrow r=9\). So the term is \(\binom{18}{9}(-2)^{9}=-\binom{18}{9}2^{9}\). Hence (D).

In \((1-2x)^{18}\), the coefficient of \(x^{k}\) is \(\binom{18}{k}(-2)^{k}\); so coefficients of \(x^{2},x^{3},x^{4}\) are \(\binom{18}{2}4=612\), \(\binom{18}{3}(-8)=-6528\), \(\binom{18}{4}16=48960\). Multiplying by \((1+ax+bx^{2})\): coefficient of \(x^{3}=(-6528)+a(612)+b(-2\cdot 18\cdot... )\). Setting the coefficients of \(x^{3}\) and \(x^{4}\) to zero and solving the two linear equations gives \(a=16\) and \(b=\dfrac{272}{3}\). Hence (C).

In \(\left(ax^{2}+\dfrac{1}{bx}\right)^{13}\), the term in \(x^{8}\) has \(26-3r=8\Rightarrow r=6\), coefficient \(\binom{13}{6}a^{7}b^{-6}\). In \(\left(ax-\dfrac{1}{bx^{2}}\right)^{13}\), the term in \(x^{-8}\) has \(13-3r=-8\Rightarrow r=7\), coefficient \(\binom{13}{7}a^{6}(-1)^{7}b^{-7}=-\binom{13}{7}a^{6}b^{-7}\). Since \(\binom{13}{6}=\binom{13}{7}\), equating gives \(a^{7}b^{-6}=-a^{6}b^{-7}\Rightarrow ab=-1\Rightarrow ab+1=0\). Hence (A).

Using \(\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}^{2}=\binom{2n}{n}\), subtract the \(r=0\) term \(\binom{n}{0}^{2}=1\). Thus \(\binom{n}{1}^{2}+\binom{n}{2}^{2}+\cdots+\binom{n}{n}^{2}=\binom{2n}{n}-1\). Hence (D).

The ratio \(\dfrac{t_{r+1}}{t_{r}}\) of consecutive terms of \((a+b)^{m}\) is \(\dfrac{m-r+1}{r}\cdot\dfrac{b}{a}\). For \((a+b)^{n+4}\), \(\dfrac{t_{6}}{t_{5}}=\dfrac{(n+4)-4}{5}\cdot\dfrac{b}{a}=\dfrac{n}{5}\cdot\dfrac{b}{a}\). For \((a+b)^{n}\), \(\dfrac{t_{5}}{t_{4}}=\dfrac{n-3}{4}\cdot\dfrac{b}{a}\). Equating: \(\dfrac{n}{5}=\dfrac{n-3}{4}\Rightarrow 4n=5n-15\Rightarrow n=15\). Hence (D).

The \((3r)^{\text{th}}\) term is \(T_{3r}=\binom{2n}{3r-1}x^{3r-1}\) and the \((r+2)^{\text{th}}\) term is \(T_{r+2}=\binom{2n}{r+1}x^{r+1}\). These are equal only if their binomial coefficients are equal: \(\binom{2n}{3r-1}=\binom{2n}{r+1}\). Rejecting \(3r-1=r+1\), take \((3r-1)+(r+1)=2n\Rightarrow 4r=2n\Rightarrow n=2r\). Hence (C).
In \((1+x)^{2n}-(1-x)^{2n}\), the even-power terms cancel and the odd-power terms double: surviving powers are \(x^{1},x^{3},\ldots,x^{2n-1}\), which is \(n\) terms. Hence (C).

Equal coefficients require \(\binom{15}{(2r+3)-1}=\binom{15}{(r-1)-1}\), i.e. \(\binom{15}{2r+2}=\binom{15}{r-2}\). Either \(2r+2=r-2\) (rejected, gives \(r=-4\)) or \((2r+2)+(r-2)=15\Rightarrow 3r=15\Rightarrow r=5\). Hence (C).
The sum \(1+(1+x)+\cdots+(1+x)^{20}=\dfrac{(1+x)^{21}-1}{x}\). The coefficient of \(x^{10}\) here equals the coefficient of \(x^{11}\) in \((1+x)^{21}\), which is \(\binom{21}{11}\). Hence (C).

Coefficients of the 2nd, 3rd, 4th terms of \((1+x)^{n}\) are \(\binom{n}{1},\binom{n}{2},\binom{n}{3}\). In AP: \(2\binom{n}{2}=\binom{n}{1}+\binom{n}{3}\Rightarrow n(n-1)=n+\dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}\). Simplifying gives \(n^{2}-9n+14=0\Rightarrow n=7\) (taking \(n\neq 2\)). The sum of coefficients of odd powers is \(2^{n-1}=2^{6}=64\). Hence (B).

Factor \(1-x-x^{2}+x^{3}=(1-x)(1-x^{2})=(1-x)^{2}(1+x)\), so the expression is \((1-x)^{12}(1+x)^{6}\). Computing the coefficient of \(x^{7}\) by convolving \((1-x)^{12}=\sum\binom{12}{i}(-1)^{i}x^{i}\) with \((1+x)^{6}=\sum\binom{6}{j}x^{j}\) over \(i+j=7\): \(\sum_{j=1}^{6}(-1)^{7-j}\binom{12}{7-j}\binom{6}{j}=-144\). Hence (A).

Equal coefficients of the \((r-5)^{\text{th}}\) and \((3r+1)^{\text{th}}\) terms of \((1+x)^{12}\) require \(\binom{12}{r-6}=\binom{12}{3r}\). Either \(r-6=3r\) (rejected, \(r=-3\)) or \((r-6)+3r=12\Rightarrow 4r=18\Rightarrow r=4.5\), which is not a valid (positive integer) term index. Hence no valid \(r\) exists. Hence (D).
Equal coefficients of \(x^{r}\) and \(x^{r+3}\) in \((1+x)^{15}\) require \(\binom{15}{r}=\binom{15}{r+3}\Rightarrow r+(r+3)=15\Rightarrow 2r=12\Rightarrow r=6\). Hence (C).

The 5th and 6th terms of \((a-2b)^{n}\) are \(T_{5}=\binom{n}{4}a^{n-4}(-2b)^{4}\) and \(T_{6}=\binom{n}{5}a^{n-5}(-2b)^{5}\). Their sum is zero: \(\binom{n}{4}a^{n-4}16b^{4}=\binom{n}{5}a^{n-5}32b^{5}\Rightarrow \dfrac{a}{b}=2\cdot\dfrac{\binom{n}{5}}{\binom{n}{4}}=2\cdot\dfrac{n-4}{5}=\dfrac{2(n-4)}{5}\). Hence (B).

In \((x+y)^{100}+(x-y)^{100}\), the odd-power-of-\(y\) terms cancel and the even-power terms double. The surviving powers of \(y\) are \(y^{0},y^{2},\ldots,y^{100}\), i.e. \(\dfrac{100}{2}+1=51\) terms. Hence (C).

The ratio \(\dfrac{T_{r}}{T_{r+1}}=\dfrac{r}{m-r+1}\cdot\dfrac{a}{b}\). So \(\dfrac{T_{2}}{T_{3}}\) in \((a+b)^{n}\) is \(\dfrac{2}{n-1}\cdot\dfrac{a}{b}\) and \(\dfrac{T_{3}}{T_{4}}\) in \((a+b)^{n+3}\) is \(\dfrac{3}{(n+3)-3+1}\cdot\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{3}{n+1}\cdot\dfrac{a}{b}\). Equating: \(\dfrac{2}{n-1}=\dfrac{3}{n+1}\Rightarrow 2(n+1)=3(n-1)\Rightarrow 2n+2=3n-3\Rightarrow n=5\). Hence (C).
Write \((27)^{999}=(28-1)^{999}=28\lambda+(-1)^{999}=28\lambda-1=7(4\lambda-1)+6\). So the remainder on division by 7 is 6. Hence (A).

Putting \(x=1\): \(3^{9}=a_{0}+a_{1}+\cdots+a_{18}\). Putting \(x=-1\): \(1=a_{0}-a_{1}+\cdots+a_{18}\). Adding and halving, \(a_{0}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{18}=\dfrac{3^{9}+1}{2}=\dfrac{19683+1}{2}=9842\), which is even (and not divisible by 3 or 9). Hence (B).
The unit digits of powers of 3 cycle as \(3,9,7,1\) (period 4). Since \(101\equiv 1\pmod 4\), \(3^{101}\) ends in 3, so \(3^{101}+1\) ends in 4. Hence (D).
The sum of coefficients is obtained by putting \(x=1\): \((1+1+1-4)^{2149}=(-1)^{2149}=-1\). Hence (B).
The unit digits of powers of 7 cycle as \(7,9,3,1\) (period 4). Since \(886\equiv 2\pmod 4\), the last digit of \(7^{886}\) is 9. Hence (B).
The sum of coefficients is obtained by putting \(x=1\): \((1+3-3)^{1143}=1^{1143}=1\). Hence (C).
Since \(2^{6}=64\equiv 1\pmod 9\) and \(1505=6\cdot 250+5\), \(2^{1505}=(2^{6})^{250}\cdot 2^{5}\equiv 1\cdot 32\equiv 32-27=5\pmod 9\). The remainder is 5. Hence (C).
The sum of coefficients is obtained by putting \(x=1\): \((a^{2}-6a+11)^{10}=1024=2^{10}\Rightarrow a^{2}-6a+11=2\Rightarrow a^{2}-6a+9=0\Rightarrow (a-3)^{2}=0\Rightarrow a=3\). Hence (D).
Factorise \(450=2\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 5^{2}\). The sum of all positive divisors is \((1+2)(1+3+9)(1+5+25)=3\cdot 13\cdot 31=1209\). Hence (A).
Every positive integer power of 5 ends in the digit 5, so \(5^{834}\) has unit digit 5. Hence (B).

Modulo 5: \(3^{4}\equiv 1\), and \(100\equiv 0\pmod 4\), so \(3^{100}\equiv 1\). Also \(2^{4}\equiv 1\), and \(50\equiv 2\pmod 4\), so \(2^{50}\equiv 2^{2}=4\). Thus \(3^{100}\times 2^{50}\equiv 1\cdot 4=4\pmod 5\). The remainder is 4. Hence (B).

The sum \(A=1+(1+x)+\cdots+(1+x)^{n}=\dfrac{(1+x)^{n+1}-1}{x}\). The coefficient of \(x^{k}\) in \(A\) equals the coefficient of \(x^{k+1}\) in \((1+x)^{n+1}\), which is \(\binom{n+1}{k+1}\). This matches none of the listed options \(\binom{n}{k},\binom{n-1}{k},\binom{n-1}{k+1}\). Hence (D).
The sum of coefficients is obtained by putting \(x=1\): \((1-3+3)^{3148}=1^{3148}=1\). Hence (C).
Since \(5^{3}=125\equiv 1\pmod{124}\) and \(124=3\cdot 41+1\), \(5^{124}=(5^{3})^{41}\cdot 5\equiv 1\cdot 5=5\pmod{124}\). The remainder is 5. Hence (A).
